LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- Media maven Oprah Winfrey earned 10 times more than Angelina Jolie last year, but the actress bumped the talk show host from the top spot on Forbes' 2009 Celebrity 100 list just released by the business magazine. Angelina Jolie has ousted Oprah Winfrey from the No. 1 spot on Forbes' 2009 Celebrity 100 list. Jolie's fame, evidenced by magazine covers and TV, radio, newspaper and Web stories, outweighed Winfrey's, giving her the edge as "the most powerful celebrity in the world" based on Forbes' formula, Forbes Senior Editor Matthew Miller said. Winfrey, who was at the top for two years straight, grossed $275 million last year, compared with Jolie's $27 million, Miller said. "We try and measure a celebrity's power, and we look at two metrics to do that," Miller said. "We look at money, and we look at fame." A world tour, which helped Madonna pull in $110 million, and a bumper crop of tabloid gossip pushed the Material Girl into the third spot, up from her 21st ranking on last year's list. Beyonce Knowles held steady in fourth, same as last year, with $87 million in income from her multiplatform empire, Miller said. Forbes leveraged the singer-actresses fame by placing her on this week's cover. A bad knee kept Tiger Woods off the PGA tour over the past year and lowered him to the fifth spot on the Forbes list. The golfer, still the highest-paid athlete in the world, was second last year. Bruce Springsteen's tour landed the Boss in sixth, while director Steven Spielberg's latest Indiana Jones movie helped him to seventh place. Actress Jennifer Aniston and her ex-husband, Brad Pitt, were eighth and ninth, respectively, on the strength of successful movies and tabloid headlines. Basketballer Kobe Bryant's endorsements and popularity, boosted by his play on the U.S. Olympic team, jumped to the 10th spot. Miller said Forbes' has spent a great amount of time compiling the list for the past decade because "celebrities play an ever increasing role in everyone's lives, whether we like it or not." "Celebrities are brands, and they are marketing to us and there's stuff we consume off of them, from movies to albums to concerts to books to speaking tours to everything in between, and we sort of all buy into it," he said. The income figures used are gross numbers and do not take into account what goes to agents, managers, taxes and expenses, Miller said. "It can be very expensive to be a celebrity," he said. "What they're taking home to their personal checking accounts is far less than their gross earnings." The list, which has been "put through our special sauce of earnings and fame," is used as a barometer of who has the real power in Hollywood, Miller said. "When you look at the components of fame and earnings, you can get a good vibe as to who's important this year and who's not," he said. "Angelina Jolie is, by far, the most famous celebrity on the planet," he said. "There's not a day that goes by where she's not on the cover of a tabloid magazine or a regular magazine. There's not day that goes by when people are not talking about her philanthropy or her relationship with Brad Pitt or her movies or her children. All of that lends to a more popular, more robust and, frankly, more valuable brand." Miller estimated that Jolie was on about 20 to 30 times more magazine covers last year than Winfrey. It's normal for celebs to fall down or off the list for a year if they are between projects, he said. One newcomer to the list of top 100 celebrities is Barack Obama, debuting at 49. Obama is the first sitting head of state to appear in Forbes' Celebrity 100 rankings. CNN's Jim Roope contributed to this report.

# Los Angeles: The City of Angels

Los Angeles, California is one of the most iconic and culturally significant cities in the United States. Known affectionately as "The City of Angels" (a translation of its Spanish name), Los Angeles is the second-most populous city in the country, trailing only New York City.

## Geography and Climate

Situated in Southern California, Los Angeles enjoys a Mediterranean climate characterized by warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters. The city sprawls across a vast basin, bordered by the Pacific Ocean to the west and surrounded by mountain ranges, including the San Gabriel Mountains to the north. This unique geography contributes to the city's famous sunshine, though it also creates challenges with air quality and traffic congestion.

## Entertainment Capital of the World

Los Angeles is synonymous with the entertainment industry. Hollywood, a neighborhood within the city, has served as the historic center of American film production since the early 20th century. Major film studios, television networks, and record labels call Los Angeles home, drawing aspiring actors, musicians, and artists from around the globe. The iconic Hollywood Sign remains a symbol of dreams and ambition.

## Cultural Diversity

Few cities can match the cultural diversity found in Los Angeles. The city is home to significant populations from Mexico, Central America, Asia, and countless other regions, creating vibrant neighborhoods like Koreatown, Little Tokyo, and Boyle Heights. This diversity is reflected in the city's culinary scene, festivals, and everyday life.

## Economic Powerhouse

Beyond entertainment, Los Angeles boasts a diverse economy encompassing technology, international trade, fashion, and tourism. The Port of Los Angeles is one of the busiest shipping ports in the nation, facilitating trade with Asia and beyond.

## Conclusion

Los Angeles, California embodies the American dream for many—a place where opportunity, creativity, and diversity converge against a backdrop of sunny skies and Pacific breezes. Despite challenges like traffic and housing costs, the city continues to attract millions who seek their own version of success beneath the famous Hollywood Sign.

On the financial side, the magazine calculates pretax income for each celebrity over a 12-month period, drawing on data from agents, managers, industry insiders, and public records. This income includes salaries, endorsement deals, royalties, and other revenue streams tied to a celebrity's public persona.

The fame component, meanwhile, is calculated using a composite score built from several media-related factors:

- **Press coverage** — the volume of print and online mentions
- **Television and radio presence** — frequency of appearances
- **Web presence** — search engine visibility and online buzz
- **Social media influence** — for the 2009 list, this was an increasingly important factor as platforms like Twitter began reshaping celebrity engagement

By blending these visibility metrics with hard income figures, Forbes attempts to capture not just who is making the most money, but who is culturally dominant in the public consciousness.

## The 2009 Results

The 2009 Celebrity 100 list reflected a media landscape still processing the aftermath of Michael Jackson's death earlier that year, alongside the continued dominance of reality television, sports superstars, and Hollywood's A-list. Figures whose earnings might have been modest compared to top-tier film stars nonetheless ranked highly due to overwhelming media saturation—illustrating Forbes' core thesis that fame itself carries measurable value independent of a person's bank account.

Conversely, some of the era's highest earners found themselves outside the top tier of the list, a testament to the idea that financial success alone doesn't guarantee cultural relevance in Forbes' formula.

## Why the List Matters

Critics have long argued that the Celebrity 100 oversimplifies fame into a spreadsheet, reducing complex cultural phenomena to a ranked list. Yet the list's enduring popularity speaks to a broader public fascination with quantifying influence in an industry—entertainment—that often resists neat categorization.

For brands, agents, and studios, the list serves as more than entertainment trivia. High rankings often translate into leverage for endorsement deals, film negotiations, and media appearances, making Forbes' formula a de facto barometer of marketability in Hollywood and beyond.

As social media continued its rise in the years following 2009, Forbes would go on to adjust its formula further, incorporating platforms like Twitter and Facebook more heavily—cementing the Celebrity 100 as an evolving mirror of how fame itself is created, measured, and monetized in the modern era.
